December: Atari Corporate Research (headed by Atari VP/Chief Scientist Alan 
Kay) established a Games Design Research Group.  Chris Crawford, previously 
Atari (Computer) Software Development Support Group supervisor, became 
Manager, Games Design Research Group.  Atari (Computer) national sales 
training manager Bill Carris would assume responsibility for the Software 
Development Support Group (replacing Crawford in the role).

December?: Linda S. Gordon, previously of Hellman, Jordan Management Company,
joined Atari (corporate) as VP special projects (assistant to the president;
reporting to Atari chairman/CEO Kassar).

December: Steven T. Mayer was VP of research and development at Atari. (NYT
12/24/81 pD2; NYT 12/31/81 pD2)

December?: The Atari Computer Division would now be known as the Atari Home
Computer Division (HCD), and it adopted the advertising slogan, "We've brought
the computer age home."

December 28: At Atari (Home Computer), Keith Schaefer had been promoted from 
National Sales Manager to sales VP (TVDigest), and Don Kurtz, previously 
manager of marketing communications, had been promoted to director of 
marketing services (see AtariConnection v2n2p1), together replacing VP sales 
& marketing Barry Berghorn who had departed the company (to Via Video, 
Inc.).  Gerald A. Ruttenbur (Jerry Ruttenbur), previously of M&M Mars 
Distributing, would join Atari (Computer) as national sales manager 
(replacing Schaefer in the role; reporting to Schaefer). (Microsoft 
Prospectus 3/13/86)

December 30: Atari said that it would cut the retail price for the 800 home
computer (with 16KiB RAM and newly "mass market packaged") to $899 from
$1,080.  Other prices were increased: The Entertainer to $110 and The
Educator to $166.

Atari claimed to have sold 300,000 400/800 computers in 1981.
(InfoWord 6/14/82 p.57)

The installed base of Atari 400/800 computers was estimated by Future
Computing, Inc. to be just over 100,000. (January 1983)

1982
January 5: In advance of the opening of the Winter CES on January 7, for the
400/800 Atari (Home Computer) announced: Pac-Man (title by Namco; 2nd quarter
1982), Centipede (2nd quarter 1982), Caverns of Mars (originally developed for
APX; 1st quarter 1982), The Bookkeeper, The Home Filing Manager.  J. Peter
Nelson was Atari (Home Computer) spokesperson. (PR) 
 
January 6: Atari announced the publication, Atari Special Editions, a catalog
of more than 400 products for the Atari computers from 117 vendors.

January 7-10: At the Winter CES in Las Vegas, for the 400 ($399/16KiB RAM)
and 800 ($899/16KiB RAM) Atari introduced Pac-Man (title by Namco; to ship
in May -Analog#6p13), Centipede (June -Analog#6p13), and Caverns of Mars
(which had only just been added to the APX product line as of December
1981; it would be the first APX title to be transferred into Atari's main
product line), announced The Bookkeeper, The Home Filing Manager, the CX85
Numerical Keypad (price tba), The Bookkeeper Kit (price tba) and The Home
Manager Kit (price tba), and again promised: Dow Jones Investment
Evaluator (never shipped), Personal Financial Management System, Atari
Macro Assembler and Program-Text Editor, Atari Microsoft BASIC.  Following
the 400 packaging theme introduced in 1981, the 800, 810, and 410 would
now ship in silver/full color packaging.  The Atari (Computer) service 
network included Authorized Atari Computer Service Centers and Atari service 
facilities in California and New Jersey. (C017535RevB) 

January?: Atari Consumer Product Service (CPS; previously: Consumer/Home 
Computer Customer Service; still headed by Jon Ebbs) had opened two new 
Regional Service Centers at 5400 Newport Dr Ste 1, Rolling Meadows IL and at 
2109 E Division St, Arlington TX.  Operations at 1340/1346 Bordeaux Dr, 
Sunnyvale CA (home of Customer Support and a Regional Service Center) would 
move to 1312 Crossman Ave, Sunnyvale CA.  (A fourth Regional Service Center 
remained at 43 Belmont Dr, Somerset NJ.)  Dave Wilson (previously: manager of 
Customer Support) would be manager of Customer Relations (representatives and 
specialists; still reporting to Ebbs).  Bill Bartlett, previously an Atari 
(Home Computer) product marketing manager, would be supervisor of customer 
relations specialists (reporting to Wilson).  Dave Menconi, previously a 
Customer Service technical support specialist (reporting to manager of 
technical support John Hahn) became a software analyst, Atari (Home Computer) 
Users' Group Support (reporting to group manager Earl Rice).

January 16: Atari held its first annual Star Award ceremony at San 
Francisco's Maxwell's Plum restaurant in Ghiradelli Square.  The Star Award 
and ASAP Contest $25,000 grand prize went to Fernando Herrera for his APX 
title, My First Alphabet.  Star Award of Merit winners: Ronald Marcuse & Lynn 
Marcuse, Sheldon Leemon, Greg Christensen (AC Spr82p12) 

January 19-22: Atari distributor Ingersoll Electronics featured the 400/800 
at the third annual Which Computer? Show, National Exhibition Centre, 
Birmingham, England.

January 25: Internal Atari memo by systems software consultant Harry Stewart 
reflected that the project previously known as "Z800" was now known as: 
"Sweet-16".  See: https://tinyurl.com/msa9hryp

Winter?: Atari shipped Atari Microsoft BASIC (programmer at Microsoft:
Ric Weiland) and the software development package, Macro Assembler and 
Program-Text Editor. (Macro Assembler developed for Atari by Sorcim; 
Program-Text Editor also released via APX)

February: Atari VP/chief scientist Alan Kay founded the Atari Sunnyvale 
Research Laboratory, which would serve as the primary home of Atari Corporate 
Research. Systems Research Group research scientists would eventually 
include: Jim Dunion, Brenda K. Laurel (previously: Atari (Home Computer) 
Manager, Software Strategy and Marketing), Jeffrey Sarnoff (previously: Atari 
(Home Computer) software architect).  The recently-established Games Design 
Research Group would be housed in the new lab, and would eventually include 
Chris Crawford (group manager), Valerie Atkinson, Douglas Crockford, Bob 
Fraser, Randall Smith, Larry Summers, Kim Whitmore, Aric Wilmunder.  The 
Research Engineering Group (projects including Amy digital audio chip) would 
eventually include: Douglas Crockford, Scott H. Foster (digital audio), Jim 
Leiterman, Tim McGuinness, Sam Nicolino (digital audio), John Howard Palevich 
(Jack Palevich) (digital audio), Gary Sikorski (Digital Audio group manager; 
director of Research Engineering, 1983-84), Dale Yocum (director of Research 
Engineering, 1982-83; previously: APX Manager), Thomas G. Zimmerman (digital 
audio).

Atari (Home Computer) director of product review and research (including APX) 
Fred Thorlin would additionally serve as APX general manager (interim basis?;
assuming the role from Yocum).

February 5: Percom Data Company announced the RFD series of floppy disk 
drives for the Atari 400/800 (PR), the first alternatives to the Atari 810.

February: New production Atari 810 disk drives would ship in the
significantly-revised "810 Analog" design. (Happy Computers ads for date,
e.g., Analog#18p14)

February 18: Atari established the subsidiary, Atari International (U.K.) 
Inc., to assume the Atari consumer products business from distributor 
Ingersoll Electronics.  John Constantine (previously general manager, Atari 
Far East Limited (in Hong Kong)) would be acting managing director.  
(Operations would launch in April.)

March 1: Atari had completed remastering and replacing inventory of all
cassette-based products to reduce background noise on the cassettes, improving
compatibility with the newer Transtek/Hong Kong version of the 410 program
recorder. (Tech Tip 5)

March 1?: Atari released the Atari Program Exchange (APX) Software Catalog
Spring Edition 1982, introducing: Family Budget, Diskette Mailing List,
Isopleth Map-Making Package, RPN Calculator Simulator, Advanced Musicsystem,
Sketchpad, Cubbyholes, Musical Computer--The Music Tutor, Starware, Wordmaker,
Block Buster, Atari Pascal Language System (by MT MicroSYSTEMS for Atari),
Extended fig-FORTH Rev. 2, GTIA Demonstration Diskette, Instedit (Microsoft
BASIC version), Keypad Controller, Speed-O-Disk. APX also introduced the book,
De Re Atari.  (Dale Yocum had still been APX Manager at printing date.)

March 12: At Atari (Home Computer) in software, Lou Tarnay remained systems
development manager.  Reports to Tarnay included telecommunication supervisor
(acting) John Curran, operating systems supervisor Paul Laughton, and 
software architecture consultant Harry Stewart.  The telecommunication group 
included Joseph B. Miller III (Joe Miller; formerly of The Authorship 
Resource, Inc. (ARI)), Vincent H. Wu, and Gin Pao Lu.
https://archive.org/details/AtariHarryStewart

March 15: Atari had announced Atari Computer Camps, "the first effort by a
major home computer manufacturer to fully sponsor summer camps for 10 to 18-
year-olds interested in computers."  Atari was to conduct eight camp sessions
during summer 1982, two in each of four locations: Pennsylvania (East
Stroudsburg State College), North Carolina (Asheville School), Wisconsin
(Lakeland College) and southern California (University of San Diego).  Each
session would last four weeks.  While Atari would provide the computer
expertise and have ultimate oversight over the camps, day-to-day operation
would be handled for Atari by Specialty Camps, Inc., an organization which had
run both theme (Weight Watchers) and traditional camps for 25 years.  Linda
Gordon was Atari (corporate) VP of special projects; Atari (Home Computer)
Educational Software Products Manager Robert Kahn was Atari Computer Camps
Curriculum Director; Ray Kassar remained Atari chairman and CEO; Peter Nelson
was manager of public relations for Atari's home computer division. (AtariAge
My/Jn82p6; DrDobbsMy82p14; InfoWorld 3/15/82p43; Interface Age 6/82 p26) 

March: Steve Mayer, previously Atari VP research and development, would 
become VP research and product development (remaining head of the Advanced 
Products Group at the Atari Advanced Products Laboratory (Atari NY Lab)). 

March: Atari (Home Computer) formed a special projects engineering group.  
Engineer Ajay Chopra, previously of Burroughs Corporation, would join Atari 
(Home Computer) as a special projects engineer.  Jim Tittsler, previously 
director of software development at International Remote Imaging Systems (and 
before that, a software engineer at Heath Company, where he had reported to 
Larry Plummer), joined Atari (Home Computer) as a special projects engineer. 
(Larry Plummer remained Atari (Home Computer) director of hardware 
engineering.)

March: John Peeke-Vout, previously of GTE Government Systems, joined Atari 
(Home Computer) as manager of international software (new position reporting 
to VP software Bruce Irvine). (jp-v fb for month) 

March: Atari Star Raiders for the 400/800 was awarded Computer Game of the
Year by Electronic Games magazine. (EG 3/82 p49) 

March 19-21: At the 7th West Coast Computer Faire in San Francisco, Atari held
their second annual invitational hospitality suite for Atari computer users'
group officers and their guests, where Atari introduced APX Atari Pascal
Language System.  About 80 persons attended, on behalf of 15 of the 200 total
groups registered with Atari Users' Group Support.  At Atari (Home Computer),
Don Kurtz was director of marketing services; Earl Rice was manager of the
users' group support program; Bonnie Umphreys was Pascal's product manager.
(AtariConnection v2n2p1)  Also at the Faire, Percom announced plans for 15 
"RFD" floppy disk drives for the Atari (to include 6 first-drive systems and 
9 add-on drive models), and introduced the RFD40-S1 single 40-track 
first-drive and the RFD40-A1 single 40-track add-on drive. (Analog #6p8; 
price list) (Only about half of the planned RFD drive models would eventually 
ship.)

March 26: Atari established the subsidiary, Atari Special Projects, Inc.
(joint ventures with Club Mediterranee SA and/or with Specialty Camps Corp.),
with offices at 1196 Borregas Ave, Sunnyvale CA (also home to the Home
Computer division and Corporate Research).  Atari (corporate) VP special
projects Linda Gordon would additionally be president of Atari Special
Projects, Inc.

March/April: The Atari Consumer Electronics Division (Atari (Consumer)) and 
the Atari International division would together be known as the Consumer 
Products Group.  Perry D. Odak, previously general manager at Jovan, Inc., 
the fragrance and cosmetics company (and before that, SVP of Worldwide 
Operations at Armour-Dial, Inc.) joined Atari as president, Consumer Products 
Group.  Atari International president Anton Bruehl would now report to Odak 
(previously: directly to Atari chairman/CEO Ray Kassar). 

April 7: Date of first draft of the Atari Sweet-16 Home Computer Product
Specifications document.  Specific computer models planned: "1000" (16KiB;
later: "1200"; never shipped) and "1000X" (64KiB; later: "1200X"; would ship
as: 1200XL)

April: Bob Fournier was an Atari (Home Computer) entertainment product 
manager.  (Brenda Laurel remained Manager, Software Strategy and Marketing.)

April: Thomas M. McDonough joined Atari (Home Computer) as SVP sales and 
marketing. (NYT 12/19/82 for date)  (Reports to McDonough would include VP 
sales Keith Schaefer and director of marketing services Don Kurtz.)  

April: Atari launched the subsidiary, Atari International (U.K.) Inc., taking 
over the Atari consumer products business from distributor Ingersoll 
Electronics.  John Constantine was acting managing director; Graham Daubney

April 16: "The Electronic and Computer Technician Vocational Education
Incentive Grants Act" hearing before the Subcommittee on Elementary,
Secondary, and Vocational Education of the Committee on Education and Labor,
U.S. House of Representatives, included testimony by Steven Mayer, Atari VP
research and product development.

April: First issue of Antic, The Atari Resource magazine, published by James

April/May: Atari shipped, then promptly pulled from the market for further
development, Personal Financial Management System. (see Analog #9p118, plus

Spring?: Atari (Home Computer) software product coodinator Brian Johnston

May 1: Through Atari Special Projects, Inc., Atari began supplying both
equipment and instructor training for the Club Mediterranee computer classroom
at Club Med Ixtapa in Mexico (replacing Computer Camp of Santa Barbara CA,
which had the role since the classroom opened in November 1981).  (Atari did
not take on the other existing Club Med computer classroom at Club Med
Kamarina, Sicily, which had opened in May 1981.)  A second Atari computer
classroom was planned for Club Med Eleuthera, the Bahamas. (InfoWorld 7/12/82
p14-16)  

May 12-13: Initial meetings between Atari chairman Ray Kassar and Rick Trow of
Rick Trow Productions (RTP).  Would lead to "Computers: Expressway to
Tomorrow" traveling multimedia assembly program for schools, under a contract
covering the 1982-83 (including fall 1982 focus group / touring unit and
winter 1983 national launch) and 83-84 school years, with an option for the 
84-85 school year.

May 14: Atari International (U.K.) Inc. (established on 2/18/82 and operating 
since April) was registered for business in the UK.  Anthony Jones, 
previously of Ingersoll (where he had headed the 400/800 marketing group 
since its inception), would be the founding Managing Director.  John 
Constantine, previously Atari International (U.K.) acting managing director, 
would be tasked with expanding Atari operations in Hong Kong.  

May: For the 400/800 Atari shipped Pac-Man (Roklan).

May: Atari (Home Computer) opened its second regional software-acquisition 
center, managed by Jerry Connelly, at: 57 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge MA.  
(Steve Gerber remained director of software product acquisition; Bruce Irvine 
remained VP software.)  While plans for additional centers were not 
announced, Atari was considering opening a "satellite facility" in New York 
City in the near future. (InfoWorld 5/24/82 p9)

May: The Atari (Home Computer) special projects group (engineers Ajay Chopra 
and Jim Tittsler) would engage in a project to develop a combination Atari 
800/SUN workstation.  (Larry Plummer remained Atari (Home Computer) director 
of hardware engineering.)

May?: Robert Kahn, previously Atari (Home Computer) Educational Software
Product Manager, became Atari Director of Special Projects (Atari Computer
Camps and Club Med initiatives; reporting to Atari (corporate) VP special
projects Linda Gordon.)  Dr. Sueann Ambron, Ed.D, previously assistant
professor of educational psychology at Stanford University, joined Atari (Home
Computer) as manager of educational software products (replacing Kahn in the
role).  (Brenda Laurel remained Manager, Software Strategy and Marketing.)

May: Engineer Rich Pasco, previously a researcher at Xerox Palo Alto Research
Center (PARC), joined Atari (Home Computer) as Manager of VLSI Development.

May 17: Atari Consumer Product Service (CPS) launched the new "Atari Service" 
branding to be used by Atari Factory Authorized Service Centers (whether 
supporting the Atari VCS, Atari home computers/peripherals, or both).  At 
branding launch there were more than 700 Atari Service centers across the 
U.S. (AtariAge Jul/Aug82 p9) 

May 25: Paul Cubbage remained Atari (Home Computer) Manager, Product Review.

June 1?: Atari released the Atari Program Exchange (APX) Product Catalog
Summer Edition 1982, introducing: Bowler's Database Rev. 2, Data Base/Report
System, Family Vehicle Expense, Recipe Search 'n Save, Calculator (moved from
Atari's main product line), Astrology, Blackjack Tutor Rev. 1.1, Going to the
Dogs, Algicalc, Elementary Biology (by MECC), Frogmaster, Instructional

Instedit Rev. 1.1, Microsoft BASIC Cross-Reference Utility, Player Generator,

the UK with the publication of the APX Software Catalogue Summer Edition

Inc.) 

June 6-9: At the Summer CES in Chicago, for the 400 ($349/16KiB RAM; 
previously: $399) and 800 ($899/16KiB RAM), Atari introduced Atari Speed 
Reading (title by Otto & Kamm), announced Music Tutor I (would ship as: 
AtariMusic I), Juggles' Rainbow (by The Learning Co.), Juggles' House (by The
Learning Co.), and TeleLink II (never shipped as a standalone release; would
ship as part of The Communicator II kit only) and introduced The Bookkeeper 
Kit ($249.95; Bookkeeper program plus CX85 Numerical Keypad), The Communicator
II kit (price tba; new 835 modem with TeleLink II), The Home Manager Kit 
(price tba; Personal Financial Management System + The Home Filing Manager).
The APX title, My First Alphabet would be re-released as part of Atari's 
standard product line.  Again promised: The Bookkeeper (standalone program),
The Home Filing Manager, Personal Financial Management System (PFMS now to 
ship winter 1983), Centipede.  Atari also introduced the Electronic Retail 
Information Center (E.R.I.C.) video disc point of sale terminal (an Atari 800 
home computer linked to a videodisc player), one of several models of point 
of purchase (POP) merchandising displayers for retailers.  Keith Schaefer was 
VP of sales for Atari's Home Computer division.  There were more than 200 
factory-authorized service centers across the U.S. for Atari computers. 
(C017535RevC) 

June: Atari president Home Computer Division Roger Badertscher departed the 
company (NYT 8/25/82) as would VP software (software engineering) Bruce 
Irvine.  (Badertscher and Irvine would co-found Mindset Corporation on 
9/27/82.)  Brenda Laurel, previously Atari (Home Computer) Manager, Software 
Strategy and Marketing (reporting to Badertscher), would join Atari Corporate 
Research in Systems Research.  Bill Carris, previously Atari (Home Computer) 
director of sales training, would become Atari (Home Computer) director of 
software marketing (replacing Laurel in the role; reporting to SVP sales and 
marketing Thomas McDonough).  Carris would remain responsible for the 
Software Development Support Group, which would be renamed, the Atari I/O 
Seminar Services Group. (AtariConnection Sum82p2&4)  Thomas Hudson would be 
promoted to national sales trainer (replacing Carris in the role).

June: Conrad Jutson, previously Atari (Consumer) VP market planning, would 
become Atari (corporate) VP product planning (reporting to chairman/CEO Ray 
Kassar).

June: Stephen M. Race (Stephen Race), previously a consultant for Arthur D. 
Little Inc., would join Atari International as product manager for computer 
hardware, in part replacing international market manager for hardware Jeff 
Burton who departed the company (to Electronic Arts).  (Anton Bruehl remained 
president of Atari International.)

June 18: Warner Communications Inc. (WCI) had elected Jac Holzman, senior 
consultant to the Office of the President of WCI and a director of Atari, 
chairman of its Panavision, Inc. subsidiary. (NYT 6/18/82)  Atari VP research 
and product development Steve Mayer would additionally become senior 
executive consultant to the office of the president of WCI (replacing Holzman 
in the role), and Mayer would also replace Holzman on the Atari board of 
directors (which still included Atari chairman Ray Kassar and Manny Gerard, 
office of the president of WCI).

June 28: Engineer John Skruch, previously of Magnuson Engineers, joined Atari 
in software product engineering (responsible for technical support of Atari 
computer software products at Atari manufacturing sites).  (Paul Malloy 
remained Atari (Consumer/Computer) SVP manufacturing.)

engineering (reporting to VP engineering Lyle Rains), became Atari (Home 
Computer) VP engineering, replacing Gene Rosen who departed the company. 
(Stubben resume)

June/July?: At Atari (Home Computer), Kevin McKinsey, previously manager of 
Industrial Design and Graphics, would remain manager of industrial design 
(reporting to VP engineering Dave Stubben).  John Fox Haag would become 
manager of publications and packaging design (assuming the role from 
McKinsey), reporting to SVP of sales and marketing Thomas M. McDonough.

July 9: Release of the Walt Disney feature film TRON, with sound effects 
design and synthesis by Frank Serafine, Serafine FX Studios, who derived some 
of the sound effects from sounds generated by an Atari 800. (Atari Connection 
v2n2 Sum82 p9-10; Compute! #28 9/82 p18-22) 

July 14: In what was believed to be the largest single order for home
computers by a school system, Dade County (Florida) had placed an order for
426 Atari 800 Home Computers and peripherals.  "This order brings the total
number of Atari Home Computers in use in Dade County schools to approximately
650," said Thomas McDonough, SVP of sales and marketing for Atari's Home
Computer Division.

July?: John Hagel III, previously of The Sequoia Group (founder and CEO), 
joined Atari (Home Computer) as VP strategic planning (to report to the 
division president).  Hagel had been hired by Warner Communications chairman 
and CEO Steve Ross.

July: Atari Corporate Research (Alan Kay, VP/chief scientist) established the 
Atari Cambridge Research Laboratory at Five Cambridge Center, 8th floor, 
Cambridge MA (Kendall Square district; adjacent to the Massachusetts 
Institute of Technology (MIT)), to engage in basic research in the tradition 
of Seymour Papert, Marvin Minsky, and the Logo Group at the MIT AI Lab.  The 
lab's Director would be Cynthia Solomon, previously VP, Research & 
Development/Co-Founder of Logo Computer Systems, Inc. (and before that, 
co-inventor of Logo, and co-founder of the MIT Logo Group); administrative 
manager: James Russell Davis; business manager: Greg Gargarian.  Researchers 
at the 35-person lab would eventually include: Max Behensky, Peter Cann, 
Susan Cotten, Jim Davis (James Raymond Davis), Lisa Delpit, Gary Drescher, 
Annette Dula, Michael Grandfield, Mark Gross, Ken Haase, Stephen Hain, Edward 
F. Hardebeck, Jay Jones, Susan Kroon, Jaron Lanier, David Levitt, Dan 
Melnechuk, Henry Minsky, Julie Minsky, Margaret R. Minsky, Bill St. Clair 
(Jan84-Mar84), Nancy Smith, Tom Trobaugh, Lauren Young.  Chief consultant: 
Marvin Minsky

July: Les Player, previously of Digital Microsystems, joined Atari 
International (U.K.) Inc. as Technical Services Manager (service, repair, and 
technical training).  Player would establish a network of Atari Independent 
Service Centres across the UK, plus an Atari Service Centre (incorporating 
national Customer Support/Product Support) which would be managed by George 
West and located at the subsidiary's headquarters in Slough.  (Anthony Jones 
remained Atari International (U.K.) managing director.)

Summer: First year of Atari Computer Camps, held at 3 locations: "Camp Atari--

Stroudsburg State College (PA).  (Camp was canceled at the fourth announced
site, "Camp Atari--Sheboygan" at Lakeland College in Sheboygan WI.)  Pricing:
$1590/4 weeks or $2790/8 weeks.

peripherals, and a Centipede coin-operated game.

agreement under which Atari was granted worldwide exclusive rights to market

August 24: John C. Cavalier was named Atari president Home Computer Division 
(replacement for the departed Roger Badertscher). (NYT 8/25)  Cavalier was 
previously VP and general manager of American Can's Dixie and Dixie/Marathon 
unit, makers of consumer paper products.  The new Home Computer Division 
headquarters would be located at 30 E. Plumeria Dr., San Jose CA (previously: 
1196 Borregas Ave., Sunnyvale CA.)  Chris J. Horseman, previously of Thorn 
EMI (and independent developer as Centaursoft), would join Atari (Home 
Computer) as VP software engineering (replacement for the departed Bruce 
Irvine; reporting to Cavalier). (Antic 7/83 for title)  Lou Tarnay, 
previously director of systems development (reporting to Irvine), would 
become director of software development (reporting to Horseman), assuming 
applications development from John Powers who would depart the company (to 
Convergent Technologies).  Doug Chorey, previously executive assistant to the 
VP of software, would be software support supervisor (new sound engineering 
and video graphics group; reporting to Horseman).  Reports to Chorey would 
include sound engineer Brad Fuller. 

August 29-December 31: "Atari Announces Discount Fares to the Computer Age.  
Save up to $60" promotion.  In the U.S., for the purchase of an Atari 400 
($299/16KiB), Atari offered a rebate of $10 for each purchase of up to six 
additional Atari computer products. 

Summer/Fall?: The Warner Communications L.A. Lab R&D unit (QUBE cable
television system development), located at 3701 Oak St., Burbank, CA ("Fantasy

Kay).  Others at the L.A. Lab would eventually include: Todor Fay, H. Robert
Newman (Rob Newman), Jim Wiefel

12 B World's Fair Dr., Somerset NJ. 

August/September: At Atari (Home Computer), engineer Ajay Chopra would be

Mark Davis, previously Atari (Consumer) special projects engineer, would join 
and lead the Atari (Home Computer) special projects unit (replacing Chopra in

manager of Heathkit & printer engineering, Zenith computer business group 
(and before that, engineering hardware manager, Heath computer engineering

combination Atari 800/SUN workstation to instead launch an effort to develop

later: 1600).

October 1: Florida National Banks of Florida, Inc. announced that it would
test Pronto, the in-home banking and information system, licensed from
Chemical Bank of New York, in selected markets beginning in the first quarter
of 1983.  Atari home computers had been utilized for initial Pronto testing,
though eventually the software would be adaptable to most of the personal
computers on the market. (PR) 

October 11: Atari had announced plans to produce home computers in Hong Kong
and Taiwan, beginning January 1983.  Production would take place at facilities
already producing games for Atari.  Employment at Atari's plant in Hong Kong
would grow from 700 to 1000.  Atari said computers produced in the Far East
would be marketed there, while the U.S. market would be served from its home
facilities in Silicon Valley. (Electronics News 11-Oct-82)

December 1?: Sherwin Gooch, previously Associate Director, Center for Music
Research, Florida State University, joined the Atari (Home Computer)
communications software products group (reporting to manager John Curran).

December 2: At Atari (Home Computer), Lou Tarnay was director of software 
development (reporting to VP software engineering Chris Horseman).  Direct 
reports to Tarnay included Paul Laughton (systems products), John Curran 
(communications products), Ken Balthaser (entertainment and education 
products), Joseph B. Miller (advanced development).  Reports to Laughton 
included Scott Scheiman (operating systems development) and Jim Cox (advanced 
consumer product development).  Reports to Balthaser included Clyde Grossman 
(entertainment product development) and Vincent Wu (education product 
development).  https://archive.org/details/AtariHarryStewart

December 3: Atari Research and the Columbia University Computer Science 
Department sponsored a free one-day public seminar on the diverse future of 
video games, "Video Games: Serious Business?" at the school's campus in New 
York City.  Guest speakers included Steve Mayer (Atari VP of research and 
development), Chris Crawford (manager of Atari's game research group), 
creative consultant Chris Cerf, and Warren Robinett (co-founder of The 
Learning Company, and formerly of Atari from 1977-79). (RePlay 1/83p38; 
InfoWorld 12/20/82 p33; Video Games Mar83 p15)

December 6: Atari announced that Parisian, Inc., a chain of nine stores in
Alabama with headquarters in Birmingham, was substituting an "electronic
catalog" for its Christmas catalog to promote its holiday selection as well as
to help make the public more familiar with home computers.  Approximately
1,700 gift suggestions had been programmed into Atari 800 computers.  Store
employees would help customers key in responses to four questions asked by the
electronic catalog about the person the customer is shopping for, and the
catalog would suggest three Christmas gifts and a stocking stuffer, each
tailored to suit the tastes of the gift recipient.  Two to four of the systems
had been installed in each of Parisian's nine stores. (PR) 

December 8: Atari announced that Perry Odak had been relieved of all his 
responsibilities as president of Atari's Consumer Products Group.  (Odak 
would become a partner in the Catalyst Technologies venture capital group, 
even as he would remain under contract with Atari until winter 1984.)  Anton 
Bruehl, president of Atari's international consumer electronic division 
(Atari International), would now report (on an interim basis) directly to 
Atari CEO Ray Kassar. (PR)

December 13: At the Plaza Hotel in New York City Atari introduced the 1200XL
home computer ("well under $1,000"), 1010 program recorder ($99; winter 1983),
1020 printer/plotter ($299; winter 1983), and 1025 printer ($549; spring
1983), promised the 835 modem apart from The Communicator II kit (spring
1983), and again promised the CX85 Numerical Keypad (spring 1983), The Home
Manager kit (The Home Filing Manager + Family Finances; winter 1983), and The
Communicator II kit.  The Programmer kit was updated to include the new Inside
Atari BASIC book (instead of Atari BASIC (Wiley Self-Teaching Guide)), and the
Entertainer kit was updated to include Pac-Man (instead of Missile Command).
The 800 would now ship with 48KiB RAM standard, and the 400 computer, 410
program recorder, 810 disk drive, 830 modem, and 850 interface module were to
remain available as well.  For 400/800/1200XL Atari introduced VisiCalc (by
Software Arts for VisiCorp; previously released by Personal Software, the
earlier name for VisiCorp), Galaxian (title by Namco), and Defender (title by
Williams Electronics), again promised Atari Speed Reading (to ship
imminently), Juggles' House (January), Juggles' Rainbow (January), and
TeleLink II (again promised apart from The Communicator II kit), and
announced: E.T. Phone Home! (March), Qix (title by Taito; February), Dig Dug
(title by Namco; April), AtariWriter (earlier: Word-Wise, see ANALOG #9p17;
March), Family Finances (enhanced combination of the two APX titles, Family
Cash Flow and Family Budget; replacement for the canceled Personal Financial
Management System; March), Timewise (RLM Micro Systems for Atari; based on
Weekly Planner from APX; March), Eastern Front (1941) (updated version on
cartridge; previous version released by APX), Star Trux (never shipped),
Superman III (never shipped), AtariMusic I (previously: Music Tutor I),
Microsoft BASIC II.  Atari also announced the Disney Education Series, to
consist of 5 programs developed & published by Disney, and distributed by
Atari, featuring Mickey Mouse, Peter Pan, and the Cheshire Cat.  Keith
Schaefer was VP of sales and John Cavalier was Atari president Home Computer
Division. (Analog#9 p 17, 117-118; VGU 1/83; PR) 

December 14: Date of internal memo from Atari software architecture 
consultant Harry Stewart titled "6402 Floppy Disk Controller Protocol" 
regarding the built-in disk drive for the "6402" computer under development 
(would be introduced as: 1450XLD). See: 
https://archive.org/details/AtariHarryStewart

December 14: At Atari International: Gerd Stoecker, previously director of 
finance, had been promoted to VP finance; Claude Nahum, previously manager of 
international financial planning & analysis (reporting to Stoecker), had been 
promoted to director of finance (still reporting to Stoecker).  (Anton Bruehl 
remained president of Atari International.)

December: Atari shipped: Galaxian, Defender, Atari Speed Reading (Learning
Multi-Systems, Inc.)

December: Atari International (U.K.) Inc. had established a network of
Independent Service Centres, supported by the Atari Service Centre at company
headquarters in Slough, using the Atari Service Factory Authorised Network
branding.  (Les Player remained Technical Services Manager, Atari 
International (U.K.).)

December 19: Atari (Home Computer) SVP of sales and marketing Thomas M.
McDonough had departed the company. (NYT 12/19/82) (to Kenyon & Eckhardt).
(John Cavalier remained Atari (Home Computer) division president.) 

December 23: Completion date for "Sweet-16 OS" Rev.11 (XL OS Rev.B for the 
Atari 1200XL).

December/January: First issue of Page 6 magazine, the U.K.'s first Atari
computer magazine.  Published by Les Ellingham.

Winter 82/83: First issue of I/O, later known as Input/Output, the magazine of
the Atari Home Computer Club (Atari International (U.K.)).

Atari sold 140,000 of its 800 computers and 220,000 of its 400 computers to 
U.S. homes in 1982, as estimated by The Yankee Group. (12/83 and 3/84) 

The worldwide installed base of Atari 400/800 was estimated by Future
Computing, Inc. to be about 500,000, with about 425,000 in the U.S. (January
1983).

1983
January 3: In West Germany, David Evans would join Atari Elektronik as 
marketing director-computer line.  (Klaus Ollmann remained Atari Elektronik 
managing director.)

January 6-9: At the Winter CES in Las Vegas, Atari announced the U.S. retail 
price for the upcoming 1200XL computer ($899; March), and announced a retail 
price reduction for the 800 ($679/48KiB RAM/no longer with Atari BASIC 
cartridge and books; previously: $899/48KiB with Atari BASIC cartridge and 
books).  Atari would further offer a $55 per unit off-invoice allowance on 
the 400 ($299 retail) to their U.S. dealers and distributors through March 
31, and offer the Programmer kit free with the purchase of an 800 through 
February 28. (VGU 2/83p14; 2/1/83 price list)  Atari introduced Atari 
introduced Mickey in the Great Outdoors by Walt Disney Productions, Paint 
(SuperBoots Software from Capital Children's Museum via Reston), and Donkey 
Kong (title by Nintendo), and featured or again promised: 1010 program 
recorder, 1020 printer/plotter, 1025 printer, Juggles' House (to ship 
imminently), Juggles' Rainbow (to ship imminently), AtariMusic I, 
AtariWriter, Family Finances, Timewise, VisiCalc, Dig Dug, Eastern Front 
(1941) (cartridge), E.T. Phone Home!, Qix, Star Trux (never shipped), 
Superman III (never shipped), Microsoft BASIC II, The Home Manager kit, The 
Communicator II kit. (see 2/1/83 price list)  Atari hired two teenagers, 
Robert Allbritton and John Dickerson (via family connections with Atari CEO 
Ray Kassar), to help pitch Atari computers at the show.

January 7: Date of the internal Atari document, "Atari 600 Home Computer Liz: 
Low Cost Computer Specification, Revision Two".  The 600 was projected to be 
available in two configurations: 16KiB RAM or 64KiB RAM.  (The project had 
been known variously as the Liz, Crazy 8, and S-8; would ship as: 600XL and 
800XL).  https://archive.org/details/AtariA600XLProductStatusMeetingHandout

January?: Steve Mayer, previously Atari VP of research and development, was 
promoted to SVP of research and development (remaining head of the Advanced 
Products Group at the Atari Advanced Products Laboratory (Atari NY Lab), 
senior executive consultant to the office of the president of Warner 
Communications Inc., and a director of Atari).

January: Keith Schaefer, previously Atari (Home Computer) VP sales (reporting 
to departed SVP sales and marketing Thomas McDonough), was promoted to SVP 
sales, and Jeffrey A. Heimbuck, previously SVP marketing for wine operations 
at Joseph E. Seagram & Sons, joined Atari (Home Computer) as SVP marketing 
and software engineering. (LATimes 10/11/83 for date)  (John Cavalier 
remained Atari (Home Computer) president.)  Reports to Heimbuck would include 
Chris Horseman (VP software engineering) and Ken Wirt (Kenneth R. Wirt) (VP 
marketing; previously: an Atari (Home Computer) intern and Stanford 
University MBA student).  Reports to Wirt would include Bill Carris (director 
of software marketing), Anthony Jones (XL line product manager), and Richard 
Moyer (director of marketing services; previously of Paul Masson (the wine 
company); replacing Don Kurtz who departed the company).  Director of product 
marketing (400/800 line) Mark Lutvak would depart the company (to Durango 
Systems).  Paul Laughton, previously Atari (Home Computer) systems products 
manager, would be promoted to director of software development (reporting to 
Horseman), replacing Lou Tarnay who departed the company (to Fox Video Games).

January?: Peter R. Ateshian, previously of Reticon, joined Atari (Home 
Computer) in engineering (digital circuit design).

January: Atari Consumer Product Service (CPS) management included: Jon D. Ebbs
(Atari VP for CPS), James W. Prather (manager, field service operations),
David S. Wilson (manager, customer relations), Ronald R. Elliot (manager,
materials & parts distribution), Julie B. Naughton (controller, CPS), John H.
Hahn (manager, technical support & publications), William B. McPhetridge
(manager, international & special markets services), Janis H. Pepper (manager,
service marketing).

January: Atari published the Atari Computer Educational Software Directory
(first edition). (p48 for date)  The back page of the catalog announced Atari
Logo, being developed by Logo Computer Systems, Inc. of Montreal, Canada, to
be exclusively manufactured for and distributed by Atari and to be available
fall 1983.

January: In France, P.E.C.F. Atari shipped the 400 computer (PAL B version 
localized with RGB output and Péritel/SCART interface). (L'Ordinateur 
Individuel #51 9/83p160) 

January: Atari shipped Juggles' House and Juggles' Rainbow.

January: Atari commenced production of the 1200XL at its plant at 1215
Borregas Ave., Sunnyvale CA.  Additionally, 400 (and 800?) production
commenced at Atari's plant in Hong Kong, while 400/800 production would
continue at 1173 Borregas Ave., Sunnyvale CA.

January?: Some Atari Consumer Product Service (CPS) operations (headquarters,
materials & parts distribution) would move into 1272 Borregas Ave, Sunnyvale
CA.

January 15: At the 2nd annual Atari Star Award banquet, held at San
Francisco's St. Francis Hotel, Atari awarded the Atari Star Award and $25,000
Grand Prize to David Buehler for his APX title, Typo Attack.  Star Special
Award of Merit winners: Douglas Crockford, Harry Koons & Art Prag, Lee Actor. 
Paul Cubbage, head of the APX Software Review team, represented APX, and Atari
(Home Computer) SVP sales Keith Schaefer made the announcement and presented
the award. (AC Spr83p10) 

January 17: Date of "Crazy 8 OS" Rev.0 (version never released; project 
would lead to: XL OS Rev.1 for the Atari 600XL/800XL).

January 18: At the Volvo Masters' tennis championship in New York's Madison
Square Garden, Atari's Home Computer Division and the Association of Tennis
Professionals unveiled the Atari-ATP Computer Ranking System.  Also, the Atari
800 was now the official computer of the ATP.

January 18-21: In the UK, Atari featured the 400/800 at the Which Computer? 
show at the Birmingham National Exhibition Centre, England, and for the 
400/800 Atari introduced/announced: Galaxian (title by Namco; January), 
Defender (title by Williams Electronics; January), Qix (title by Taito; 
February), E.T. Phone Home! (March), Dig Dug (title by Namco; March), 
Superman III (June; never shipped), Soccer (spring; never shipped), Eastern 
Front (1941) (cartridge; June), Star Trux (June; never shipped).

January 19: Atari was considering a new high-end "6402" computer project 
(would be introduced as: 1450XLD) which would include built-in disk drive, 
modem, and voice synthesizer.  See: 
https://archive.org/details/AtariHarryStewart

January 20: Logo Computer Systems, Inc. (LCSI) and Atari jointly announced
Atari Logo for the 400/800/1200XL.

January 24: A panel presentation at the Project BEST (Basic Education Skills 
through Technology) teleconference, originating from the Association for 
Educational Communications and Technology (AECT) convention in New Orleans, 
featured Atari (Home Computer) National Manager of Educational Marketing 
Chris Bowman. 

January 28: Date of "Crazy 8 OS" Rev.1 (version never released; project 
would lead to: XL OS Rev.1 for the Atari 600XL/800XL).

January 28: Atari would commence development work on the "1201" ("6402"
feature set except disk drive; would be introduced as: 1400XL).  See:
http://atariage.com/forums/topic/98872-atari-vaxs-being-moved/

January 31: Atari announced the appointment of Dr. Marcian E. Hoff, Jr. (Ted 
Hoff), with Intel since 1968 and previously Intel manager of applications 
research, as VP of research and development, a newly created position to lead 
research efforts for Atari's three divisions: home computers, home video 
games and coin-operated video games.  Hoff would report directly to Atari's 
chairman, Raymond E. Kassar. (NYT 2/1/83; WSJ 2/1/83)  Reports to Hoff would 
include Alan Kay (VP/chief scientist for basic research) and Gary Summers (VP 
semiconductor development and General Manager, Atari Semiconductor Group) 
(both of whom had previously reported directly to Kassar).

Winter: Dennis Groth, previously Atari EVP and CFO, became EVP and president 
of the Consumer Products Group (replacement for the departed Perry Odak).  
(Reports to Groth would include Atari International president Anton Bruehl.)  

February 7: Atari had announced that they were now shipping VisiCalc.

February 9: A.J. Sekel (Andy Sekel), previously of Pizza Hut, had joined Atari
(Home Computer) as manager of press relations (NYT), having replaced 
J. Peter Nelson who had departed the company.

February: Atari launched the "Computers: Expressway to Tomorrow" traveling
multimedia assembly program, produced by Rick Trow Productions (RTP), offered
free of charge to junior and senior high schools in the U.S.  Using two 16-
millimeter screens (J. Charles Sterin (Chuck Sterin), filmmaker) and a live
actor, the program featured an exploration of the past, present and future of
computers in society.  The show would be presented to 1.2 million students at
nearly 1400 public and private schools through June 1983, with plans to reach
4000 schools and 3.8 million students by December 1984.  RTP had dedicated 9
of its 15-20 touring units to the Atari program. (VGU 1/83p4; AtariConnection 
v3n1p11; AtariAge v2n1p9; PersonalComputing 9/83p32-34; Review: A Catalog of 
Atari Learning Systems p3; InfoWorld 6/13/83p22)

February?: Atari shipped: Numerical Keypad (CX85; $124.95)

February: Atari shipped: Qix (VGU)

February 22: Atari announced that manufacturing for its Home Computer Division
would be consolidated mainly in Hong Kong and Taiwan, where Atari already
manufactured consumer electronics products, and announced 1,700 layoffs.
Atari said that 600 workers in its home video game operation were laid off
effective immediately, and that another 1,100 in the home computer division
would lose their jobs over the next four months. "Manufacturing for home
computers and video games will come to a virtual halt here in the United
States by July," Atari said.  

March 1?: Atari released the Atari Program Exchange (APX) Product Catalog
Spring Edition 1983, introducing: Atspeller, Typit, Fingerspelling, Escape to
Equatus, Math Mission, My Spelling Easel, Teasers by Tobbs, Three R Math
Classroom Kit, Catterpiggle, Diggerbonk, Getaway!, Impact, Microsailing,
Chameleon CRT Terminal Emulator (New Version), Hex-A-Bug.  Fred Thorlin was
APX director; product review manager: Paul Cubbage.  In the UK Atari would 
publish the APX Software Catalogue Spring Edition 1983.

March 4: The Atari International marketing office in Montreux, Switzerland 
employed four full-time staff members, led by Claude Nobs (European 
Coordinator) and Yves Greppin (engineer and European Software Coordinator). 
(L'Est Vaudois 3/4/83) 

March 7: Jim Romanos, previously Atari (Home Computer) software product test 
manager, had been promoted to director of software development (reporting to 
VP software engineering Chris Horseman), replacing Paul Laughton who had 
departed the company (to Fox Video Games).  Direct reports to Romanos: Ken 
Balthaser (applications), John Curran (systems and telecommunications), Doug 
Chorey (software support: sound and video graphics).  Reports to Balthaser: 
Clyde Grossman (entertainment applications), Jim Cox (advanced home 
applications).  Reports to Curran: Scott Scheiman (systems), Sherwin Gooch 
(telecommunications, replacing Curran in the role).  Technical staff 
reporting to Romanos: Joe Miller, Greg Riker, Lane Winner.

https://archive.org/details/AtariHarryStewart

March 8: Penril Corp., a Rockville-based electronics firm, had won a $4
million contract to provide low-cost communications modems to Atari.  Penril
was expected to ship roughly 100,000 modems (Atari 1030) by the middle of
1984, with delivery beginning July 1983. (Washington Post 3/8)

March 8-April 4: Atari featured the 400/800 at the Daily Mail Ideal Home
Exhibition, Earls Court, London.

Chris Horseman included Jim Romanos (director internal development), Paul

Peter Rosenthal would depart the company (to DesignWare, Inc.).  Robert D. 
Cory, previously of the Boston Consulting Group (and before that, the 
Standard Research Institute), would join Atari (Home Computer) as director of 
business planning (replacing Rosenthal in the role).

March: Atari (Home Computer) director of finance Bill Kaiser departed the
company (to Electronic Arts).

The Board, 6/83 p26 for month), and shipped the 1010 program recorder 
($99.95).

March: In France, Jean Richen would join P.E.C.F. Atari as director of 
marketing, replacing Christian Paternot who departed the company (to the

March 18-20: At the 8th Annual West Coast Computer Faire at the Brooks
Convention Hall and Civic Center in San Francisco, Atari introduced the 1050
disk drive (with DOS 2.0S; spring 1983), again promised the 1020
printer/plotter (spring 1983), 1025 printer (spring 1983), 835 modem, and The
Communicator II kit, featured the 1010 program recorder (1200XL sales flyer),
featured Dig Dug, E.T. Phone Home!, Qix, and AtariWriter, and introduced Atari
Logo (Brian Silverman of LCSI for Atari).  Atari announced a $50 rebate,
starting April 15, for the purchase of a 400 computer, and hinted that the 400
was soon to be replaced by a new model (presumptive name: 600XL).

March 20: In West Germany, Steve Molyneux, previously Atari Elektronik 
Vertriebsgesellschaft mbH software marketing manager, had become software 
development manager, making Atari Elektronik Atari's second international 
software development center (after London, established 10/82). (WashPost 
3/20/83)  (John Peeke-Vout remained Atari (Home Computer) director of

March 23: In the Netherlands, Atari International (Benelux) B.V. expanded to 
a new headquarters at: Atoomweg 480, Utrecht.  J. (Han) van Egdom would be

Operators Expo '83 (AOE '83) at the O'Hare Exposition Center in Chicago.

March 26: Jack Perron had become Acting Manager, Product Review, APX,
replacing Paul Cubbage who departed the company (to Mindset).

Winter/Spring: Atari (Home Computer) launched the Atari Instructional

Spring: Atari shipped: The Home Manager kit, Mickey in the Great Outdoors
(Walt Disney Telecommunications & Non-Theatrical Company),

Spring: Anthony Jones, previously Atari (Home Computer) XL line product 
manager (reporting to VP marketing Ken Wirt), became Atari (Home Computer) 
director of product planning (reporting to division president John 
Cavalier).  Andrew Soderberg was promoted to XL line product manager 
(replacing Jones in the role; reporting to Wirt).  Thomas Hudson, previously

Sally Bowman, previously Atari (Home Computer) manager, direct marketing, 
became an Atari (Home Computer) group product manager (reporting to

Spring: There were now eight Atari computer classrooms in Club Med villages:

Copper Mountain in the Colorado Rockies near Denver; Dom Miguel in Marbella,

Spring: Steve Gerber and John Peeke-Vout swapped roles for Atari (Home 
Computer): Gerber (previously: director of software product acquisition, USA) 
would be director of international software and head of the Software 
Development Group at the Software Development Centre located at Atari 
International (U.K.) Inc. (I/O#4p4), while Peeke-Vout (previously: director

manager (reporting to Atari Service Centre head George West), would be 
software development manager (reporting to Gerber). (I/O#4p4)  Shamus Kelly 
would become product support manager (replacing Norledge in the role; 
reporting to West).

May 4: Warner Communications Inc. (WCI) established the subsidiary, WCI Labs 
Inc.  The Atari Advanced Development Laboratory (Atari NY Lab) at 300 E. 42nd 
St. Fl 6/10, New York NY, home of the Atari Advanced Development Group, would 
become the facility of WCI Labs, which would serve Atari as well as other 
units of WCI.  Steve Mayer, previously Atari SVP research and development, 
would be president of WCI Labs, and would also remain senior executive 
consultant to the office of the president of WCI and a director of Atari.

May 8: Dr. Alfred L. Moye, formerly the U.S. Dept. of Higher Education's

May?: At Atari Consumer Product Service (CPS): Dave Wilson, previously manager

reporting to Bartlett). (AnticNov83p20-21)

May?: Atari (corporate) VP special projects Linda Gordon assumed 
responsibility for educational marketing of Atari computers (InfoWorld 
2/27/84 p105) from Atari (Home Computer) national manager of educational 
marketing Chris Bowman who departed the company (to Apple Computer).  Mike 
Knoblauh, previously Atari (Home Computer) manager, Atari Instructional 
Material Service (AIMS) (reporting to Bowman), would be manager of 
educational software acquisition and development (reporting to Gordon).  Mark 
O. McCrackin would be educational product manager (reporting to Gordon) 
(ScientificAmerican Jan84pC6), replacing Atari (Home Computer) manager of 
educational software products Sueann Ambron who departed the company (to 
Human Engineered Software (HesWare); she would join Apple Computer in 1984). 
Alfred Moyé, recently announced as the new Atari (Home Computer) National 
Educational Sales Manager, would now report to Gordon.

May: Atari (Home Computer) entertainment product manager Bob Fournier would 
depart the company (to HesWare).

May: Atari discontinued production of the 400 (both at 1173 Borregas Ave.,
Sunnyvale CA and at Atari's plant in Hong Kong).  Atari also discontinued
domestic production of the 800, and Atari's plant at 1173 Borregas Ave. would
be repurposed.  800 production would commence (continue?) at the Hong Kong
plant (for the short-term).

May: Atari discontinued domestic production of the 1200XL (1215 Borregas Ave.,
Sunnyvale CA).  1200XL production would continue by Atari Taiwan Manufacturing
Corp. (ATMC).

May?: Production of the 1050 disk drive commenced in Singapore by Atari-PCI
Enterprises Pte. Ltd.

May: Atari shipped: E.T. Phone Home! (VGU) 

May 15-20: At the Twenty-Fourth Annual Conference of the Australian College of
Education held in Sydney Australia, Atari International marketing manager for
software Nancy Garrison revealed that the 1200XL would not be released in 
Australia.  Rather, a new range of more powerful machines was to debut at the 
upcoming (June) CES in the U.S. (SydneyMorningHerald 5/30/83)

May 15-October 31: In the U.S. Atari offered a $100 rebate for the purchase 
of an Atari 800 home computer.

May 18-September 12: In Paris, at the Forum of the Pompidou Centre, the Au
temps de l'espace (In Space Time) exhibit by the Centre de creation
industrielle (CCI; Industrial Creation Center) included components (including
Atari 800 and software) from the ongoing TEME (Totally Enclosed Modular
Environment) project in human ecology at Greenfield Community College (MA),
with financial support from Atari via the Atari Institute for Educational
Action Research.  485,270 would visit the exhibit over 85 days. (Antic v2n6) 

May 20: Atari launched Atari International (Italy) Inc. with a press 
conference held at the Hotel Principe di Savoia in Milan.  The new subsidiary 
was Atari's fifth in Europe (France, West Germany, the United Kingdom, and 
Holland), and would replace Italian Atari computer distributor Adveico.  
Representing Atari at the event: Anton Bruehl (president of Atari 
International), Alan Kay (Atari VP/chief scientist), Manlio Allegra 
(assistant to Bruehl), and Massimo Ruosi (Direttore Generale (general 
manager) for Italy; previously of Proctor & Gamble in Italy).  Also: Vittorio 
Vitaletti would be sales director, and Ernesto Zanzi would be Direttore 
amministrativo (controller). (MCmicrocomputer #21 p14-16)

May 22-24: 110 educators attended the "Video games and human development: a 
research agenda for the 80's" symposium, Gutman Library, Harvard Graduate 
School of Education, Cambridge MA.  The conference had been organized by 
librarian Inabeth Miller at the suggestion of executives of Atari, and the 
Atari Institute for Educational Action Research had provided $40,000 to help 
underwrite the conference's administrative costs.  Alan Kay, chief scientist 
of Atari, closed the conference.

May 27: Atari (Home Computer) software architecture consultant Harry Stewart 
departed the company.  See: https://tinyurl.com/452wc96p

June 1: Atari reduced the U.S. retail price for the 400 from $299 to $149 
(before ongoing $50 rebate offer), reduced the U.S. retail price for the 800 
from $679 to $499 (before ongoing $100 rebate offer), and reduced the U.S. 
retail price for the 1200XL from $899 to $549 (before ongoing $100 rebate 
offer).

June 1?: Atari released the Atari Program Exchange (APX) Product Catalog

16KiB versions).  Fred Thorlin was APX director; product review manager: Jack
Perron.

June 1: Atari announced the consolidation of its Consumer Electronics (Atari 
(Consumer)) and Home Computer divisions into three new business units: Atari 
Products Co. (marketing and engineering), Atari Sales & Distribution Co., and 
Atari Manufacturing Co.  John Cavalier, previously Home Computer Division 
president, would be president of Atari Products Co.; Donald Kingsborough, 
previously Atari (Consumer) EVP sales and marketing, would be president of 
Atari Sales & Distribution Co.; Paul Malloy, previously Consumer/Home 
Computer SVP manufacturing, would be president of Atari Manufacturing Co.  
Cavalier, Kingsborough, and Malloy would each report to Atari chairman/CEO 
Ray Kassar, as would the presidents of the three remaining Atari divisions, 
including Atari International. (WSJ 6/2p20)  

Additional reports to Atari (Coin-Op) VP creative development Lyle Rains 
would include Chris Horseman (VP advanced games; previously: Atari (Home 
Computer) VP software engineering).

Responsibility for international sales of computer products would remain with 
Atari International, while responsibility for international marketing of 
computer products would be shifted from Atari International to Atari Products 
Co.

Reports to Cavalier would include: Jeffrey Heimbuck (SVP domestic and 
international marketing and engineering), David Ruckert (SVP entertainment 
software marketing (PR 10/10/83 for title), Fred Simon (SVP software 
marketing (computer software)) (VGU 10/83 p105 for title); previously: VP of 
the software division of Walt Disney Telecommunications and Non-Theatrical 
Company), John Hagel (VP strategic planning), Robert Cory (director of 
business development), Anthony Jones (director of product planning).

Reports to Heimbuck would include: Michel Ebertin (VP software engineering; 
previously: Atari (Consumer) VP engineering; assuming computer software 
engineering from Horseman), Dave Stubben (VP hardware engineering; 
previously: Atari (Home Computer) VP engineering), Ken Wirt (VP computer 
hardware marketing), and John Constantine (director of international 
marketing -see June 2).

Reports to Ruckert would include West Shell III (director of product 
marketing of games for Atari computers). (ArtofAtari p313)  

Reports to Simon would include Colette Weil (Director, Marketing, Home 
Applications and Children's Software; previously: Director, Corporate Market 
and Consumer Research), Fred Thorlin (director, APX), John Peeke-Vout 
(director, external software development), Steve Gerber (director, 
international software).

Reports to Kingsborough would include: Keith Schaefer (SVP computer sales), 
Conrad Jutson (SVP planning and distribution; previously: corporate VP 
product planning), Jon Ebbs (Consumer Product Service)

Departures from Atari (Home Computer) would include: group product manager

Atari (Home Computer) director of software marketing, transferred to Atari 
(Coin-Op) in marketing/special projects (Atari Adventure concept?).  

June 2: Atari had named W. Thomas Bayha (William T. Bayha), previously of 
Sterling Drug International, as managing director of its Hong Kong subsidiary 
(Atari International (Hong Kong) Limited), replacing John Constantine who was 
to join Atari's international marketing staff in Sunnyvale CA (WSJ 6/2p20) as

June 5-8: At the Summer CES held at McCormick Place in Chicago, where Atari
also hosted a nearby reception for customers at The First Chicago Center, One
First National Plaza on Sunday night, June 5, Atari introduced the 600XL home
computer ($199; to ship in July), the 800XL home computer (price to be
announced; August), the 1400XL home computer (price to be announced;
September; never shipped), and the 1450XLD home computer (price to be
announced; October; never shipped) with DOS III (later: DOS 3).  The 1050 disk
drive, currently shipping with DOS 2.0S, was to ship with DOS III by the end
of summer.  Also introduced: 1027 printer, 1030 modem (fall) with ModemLink.
Three computer expansion devices were introduced (each due in the fall): CP/M
Module with CP/M 2.2 (never shipped), Atari Expansion Box (later: 1090 XL
Expansion System; never shipped), 64K Memory Module (for the 600XL; would ship
as: 1064 Memory Module). (PR)  Also featured: 1020 printer/plotter, 1025
printer.  Accessories introduced: Touch Tablet (CX77; fall) with graphics
tablet cassette program (would ship as: AtariArtist on cartridge), Trak-Ball
(CX80; fall), Light Pen (CX75).  Announced for future introduction:
Superjoystick / Ultimate Joystick (CX60; never introduced).  The 2600 Remote
Control Wireless Joysticks (CX42) package was to be updated for marketing for
Atari home computers (package never updated).  Also featured: Numerical Keypad
(CX85).  Atari announced three All-In-One-Pak kits (each due in the fall): the
Writing System (would ship as: AtariWriter System), the Programming System
(never shipped) and the Entertainment System (never shipped).  Five Add-A-Pak
kits were featured or announced: The Communicator II (July; the 835 modem was
no longer promised to ship separately), the Atari Accountant (new name for The
Bookkeeper kit; never shipped under the new name), the Home Manager, the
Arcade Champ (August), the BASIC Tutor I (August).  Software introduced:
Tennis, Soccer (never shipped), Football, Pole Position (title by Namco),
Joust (title by Williams Electronics), Donkey Kong Junior (title by Nintendo),
Ms. Pac-Man (title by Namco), Pengo (title by Sega Enterprises), Robotron:
2084 (title by Williams Electronics), AtariMusic II: Major Scales and Keys.
Announced/previewed: The Mysteries of Wonderland (Disney; never shipped),
Peter Pan's Daring Escape (Roklan for Walt Disney Productions; never shipped).
Announced/simulated: Battlezone (title would be shipped by Atari Corporation
in 1988), Tempest (never shipped), Xevious (title by Namco; never shipped).
Again promised: AtariMusic I, TeleLink II (again promised apart from The
Communicator II kit), Superman III, Atari Logo.  (No longer promised: Star
Trux.)  Atari also introduced Alan Alda as spokesperson for Atari computers,
in an arrangement to extend for the next 5 years.
(hear: https://archive.org/details/alan-alda-atari-ces-1983 )
(CN 7/83 p3-7; Analog #13)

August 15: Following a 1-week visit by incoming chairman/CEO James Morgan 
(August 1-5?), Atari had reorganized home computer and video game 
operations.  The operating companies Atari Products Co., Atari Sales & 
Distribution Co. and Atari Manufacturing Co. had been dissolved and replaced 
with a new operating group, designated Atari Products, comprised of five 
divisions: Management (marketing operations; John Cavalier, president), Sales 
(Donald Kingsborough, president), Manufacturing (Paul Malloy, president), 
Engineering (including product development; John Farrand, president, in a new

president would report to the chairman/CEO.  Other reports to the 
chairman/CEO still included Ted Hoff (SVP technology).  (Emanuel Gerard, 
Warner Communications Inc. (WCI) office of the president, remained Atari 
interim CEO.)

Manager of Strategic Planning Norm Smothers would now report to Farrand 
(previously: to the CEO).  John Hagel, previously Atari Products Co. VP 
strategic planning (reporting to Cavalier), had become Atari (Corporate) VP 
strategic planning (EN 8/15) (replacing Smothers in the role).

Keith Schaefer, previously Atari Sales & Distribution Co. SVP computer sales, 
would be promoted to Atari Products Sales EVP (still reporting to 
Kingsborough).  Conrad Jutson, previously Atari Products Co. VP product 
planning (reporting to Cavalier), would be Atari Products Sales SVP planning 
and distribution (reporting to Kingsborough).  

Atari Products Management reports to Cavalier would include: Jeffrey Heimbuck

Atari Products Engineering reports to Farrand would include VP Michel Ebertin

September 22: Atari, Inc. and General Foods announced a multi-million dollar

conducted in Los Angeles; Denver; Chicago; Houston; New Orleans; Atlanta; St.
Louis; and Newark, N.J.  At each stop on the tour computer training experts
would present 80 hours of free tutorials especially designed for Catch-On-To-
Computers by the People's Computer Co., a non-profit company.  In addition,
weekend open houses were scheduled to provide family members and any
interested individuals the opportunity to operate the computers under
supervision.  Aside from the classes, Atari and Post Cereals would offer
schools and other membership organizations the opportunity to exchange a
specified number of Post Cereals proof-of-purchase box tops for a wide range
of Atari equipment, expansion devices and a wide selection of educational
software.  The year-long national program would kick off Sept. 30th with a
mailing of catalogs to more than 91,000 schools.  A simultaneous direct
mailing to 41 million homes -- approximately half of all U.S. households --
would announce the promotion to consumers and identify the participating Post
brands and Atari products.  Linda Gordon was SVP of the Atari education group.
(PR) 

September 23: The two Atari Center locations (Cupertino CA and New York NY)
both closed at the end of the 90-day trial period for the program. (InfoWorld
10/24/83 p16) 

September 28-October 2: Atari featured the XL range of home computers
(600XL/800XL) and products, including the new Touch Tablet (CX77) and Light
Pen (CX75), at the Sixth Personal Computer World Show (PCW), Barbican Centre,
London.

October 7: Atari Products Management president John Cavalier departed the 
company (to Apple Computer). (NYT 10/11; WSJ 10/11; EN 10/17) (James Morgan 
remained Atari chairman/CEO.)

October 10: Atari Products Management SVP hardware marketing Jeffrey Heimbuck 
had departed the company (to Koala Technologies Corp.).  Atari announced the 
appointment of David Ruckert, previously Atari Products Management SVP of 
entertainment software marketing (reporting to departed division president 
John Cavalier), as SVP of Atari Products Management, the marketing arm for 
home computers and video games (replacement for Cavalier; reporting directly 
to Atari chairman and CEO James J. Morgan).  Fred Simon (previously: SVP 
software marketing, reporting to Cavalier) was named SVP of computer 
marketing, responsible for the marketing of computer hardware and software.  
Philip Restaino (previously: director of marketing for game hardware, 
reporting to Heimbuck) was named VP of games marketing, in charge of 
marketing game hardware and game software used on Atari hardware.  Simon, 
Restaino, and Linda Gordon, who remained SVP of education, would each report 
to Ruckert. (PR)  West Shell (director, game software for Atari computers) 
would now report to Restaino (previously: to Ruckert).

Ken Wirt, previously Atari Products Management VP computer hardware marketing 
and AtariSoft (reporting to Heimbuck), would be Atari Products Sales VP for 
AtariSoft.  Don Thorson, formerly of Atari (Consumer) until 1980, would join 
Atari Products Management as director of computer hardware marketing 
(replacing Wirt in the role, but reporting to Simon).  XL computer line 
product manager Andrew Soderberg would depart the company along with product 
manager Thomas Hudson (both to ViMart).  Steve Arnold, previously Atari 
Products Management director, AtariSoft (reporting to Wirt), would be VP 
computer software marketing (including home applications and children's 
software; reporting to Simon), assuming home applications and children's 
software from Colette Weil who departed the company (to CompuFill 
Corporation, the subsidiary of McKesson Corporation). 
 
October 12: The Washington Post reported (p.D11) on Atari's plans to

computer nearing introduction was to be both IBM PC and Atari XL compatible, 
was to be built by Toshiba for Atari, and was planned to be introduced as the 
Atari 1600 (never introduced).

November 2: Report that Atari announced that because of production snags in

after the first of the year. (WSJ 11/2/1983 p.2)

January 23: James J. Morgan, chairman and CEO Atari, Inc., announced an 
organizational realignment of the company.  John Farrand, previously Atari 
(Coin-Op) president and Atari Products Engineering president, was named 
president of Atari, Inc. and president and COO of Atari Products Co. (both 
newly created positions; reporting to Morgan).  Atari Products Co. was a new 
operating division of Atari, comprised of sales and marketing, research and 
development, software development, product engineering and manufacturing, 
plus the coin-operated games unit.  Donald Kingsborough and David Ruckert 
were named Atari Products Co. EVPs of sales and marketing, respectively (each 
now reporting to Farrand).  Paul Malloy and Marcian E. "Ted" Hoff Jr. were 
named Atari Products Co. EVPs of operations/product engineering and 
R&D/product development, respectively (each now reporting to Farrand).  Steve 
Calfee was named Atari Products Co. SVP for entertainment software (consumer 
game engineering; still reporting to Farrand). (PR)

Alan Kay (VP/chief scientist) and Steve Bristow (VP product engineering 
Computer division) were named to the newly created, highest ranking technical 
position in the company: "Atari Fellow"

Reports to Morgan would also include Anton Bruehl (president of
Atari International, previously known as Atari Products International).

January 25: Atari had launched the "Eskimo" Notebook XL computer project.  
(Steve Bristow remained Atari Products Co. VP product engineering Computer 
division and an Atari Fellow.)

(for date: RCA/Columbia PR 4/5/1985) (Anton Bruehl remained president of

April: Fred Simon, previously Atari Products Co. SVP of computer marketing, 
would remain VP computer hardware and software marketing (Electronic News 
6/4/84) (still reporting to EVP marketing David Ruckert).  Philip Restaino, 
previously VP games marketing (hardware and software), would be promoted to 
SVP games marketing (hardware and software; still reporting to Ruckert).  
West Shell, previously director of games marketing for Atari computers 
(reporting to Restaino), would become director of computer software marketing 
(reporting to Simon), in part replacing John Peeke-Vout who departed the

December.).  Joel Oberman, previously director of software product marketing 
for Atari game hardware (reporting to Restaino), would be director of game 
software marketing for Atari game/computer hardware (assuming games for Atari 
computers from Shell; still reporting to Restaino).

April: Atari Products Co. VP administration Gerry Leneweaver departed the 
company (to Union Mutual Life Insurance Company).

home computers in 1985 by Epyx (North America) and Activision (Europe).)

May 27-30: At CETEX 84 (Consumer Electronics Trade Exhibition) held at Earls

May 28: In Hong Kong, Atari was folding its joint production venture with The 
Wong's Electronics Company, in which Atari owned a 51% interest, and was 
pulling out of a commitment with Chelco Sound, Inc., under which Chelco built 
the 600XL and 800XL home computers for the U.S. market.  Atari would continue 
to operate Atari Taiwan Manufacturing Corp. (ATMC), and was adding 800XL 
production there.  Ben Wong, the general manager of Atari-Wong Co., said that 
ongoing 800XL (for international markets) manufacturing there would cease by 
the end of June; after that, Wong's Electronics would make some Atari disk 
drives at other Wong facilities.  The U.S. dealer price for the 800XL had 
been cut to $217 from $280.  (EN 5/28)

Privately previewed: the (revised) 1090 XL Expansion System (formerly:
Expansion Box; to ship with one XL 64K RAM Card).  Atari also announced they
had "begun developing ties with independent firms to create software for a new
high-end computer for introduction in the second half of 1984."  The new
machine (unnamed; previously: 1450XLD), previewed privately to software
developers, was to include "a built-in, double-sided, dual density disk drive
that stores 352 kilobytes of RAM....(that) operates five times faster than a
disk drive previously planned in a computer announced a year ago (the old 1400
series)."  Also to be built-in: a 300 baud modem, telecommunications software
and a mini-database called The Grapevine, an enhanced speech synthesis chip
(upgrade from the old 1400 series), and 64K RAM.  (While the larger-capacity
built-in disk drive would not be supported by DOS 3, it would be supported by
the new "QDOS".)

At Atari Products Co., Dave Ruckert remained head (EVP) of marketing. (WSJ 
6/4)  Atari had just laid off 700 to 800 of the employees at its 
headquarters, with another 200 to 300 expected to be let go soon.  Departures 
had included VP computer hardware and software marketing Fred Simon (who had 
reported to Ruckert), director of computer hardware marketing John Hahn (who 
had reported to Simon), VP of semiconductor development (founder/head of ASG, 
the Atari Semiconductor Group) Gary Summers (who had reported to EVP research 
and development Ted Hoff), and former sales EVP Don Kingsborough (to 
Coleco).  David Wilson and Bill Bartlett of Customer Service, Consumer 
Product Service (CPS) had also departed the company. (Electronic News 6/4; 
TVDigest 6/11p22; SLCC 6/84)

replacing Gerd Stoecker who departed the company (to Tandem Computers).  

July 11: Tramel Technology, Ltd. filed a Certificate of Amendment to its
Articles of Incorporation changing the corporate name to: Atari, Corp.

August 7: Tandon Corp. announced it had reached agreement in principle for the
sale of up to $130.5 million in floppy disk drive and subsystem products to
Atari Corp.  Deliveries, which were subject to definitive purchase orders from
Atari, had begun and were scheduled to continue through the first half of
calendar 1985.

August 13: Date of internal Atari memo detailing plans for 5 new XL computers:
  1. "XL": The 64K 800XL with 3.5" FDD support and new DOS.
  2. "XL/Writer": A 64K computer with integral 80 column monochrome monitor,
     3.5" FDD, letter quality printer, and word processing software.
  3. "XL/CMOS": A portable 64K computer with built-in word processor, 3.5" FDD
     support, new DOS and 40/80 column optional LCD.
  4. "XL/M": An XL with AMY built-in. (The music machine).
  5. "XL/P": A 128K RAM version of the XL.
In addition, a 3.5" drive and a color monitor were planned.  Phil Suen was
director of XL computer engineering; Tom Brightman was VP engineering. 
https://tinyurl.com/5n7yk987

August: Atari marketing director West Shell departed the company (to The

August 25-26: TariCon '84, the first Atari-only computer fair, was held at

MACE (Mike Lechkun of the Michigan Atari Computer Enthusiasts).  About 1800
attended.  (Atari did not attend.)

August 27: Atari, Corp. stated, "Atari plans to manufacture and supply the
Atari 800XL family computer, satisfying the overwhelming and increased demand
for that product with aggressive, competitive pricing through the end of
1984."  Atari said that it had already lowered the wholesale price for the
800XL (without providing specifics).

September 9: Date of internal Atari memo detailing plans for 3 new XL
computers, with each new machine representing a step forward in cost
reduction:
  1. 800XLF incorporating FREDDIE.  
      - SECAM version due Oct 1984; NTSC/PAL versions due Nov 1984
  2. 900XLF incorporating a new keyboard and housing design
      - NTSC/PAL versions due Dec 1984; SECAM version due Feb 1985
        (would ship as: 65XE)
  3. 900XLKF incorporating KERI (function of ANTIC+GTIA+POKEY)
      - NTSC/PAL versions due Jan 1985 (SECAM version not planned)
A new cost-reduced 1050 compatible disk drive was also planned:
 - Either 3.5" or 5.25"; 163KiB capacity; 38.4Kbps transfer rate

September 11: Atari Games, Inc. (the former Atari, Inc.) was awarded U.S.
patent 4,471,463 for 6 claims by inventors Steven T. Mayer, Jay G. Miner,
Douglas G. Neubauer, and Joseph C. Decuir regarding their "Data processing
system with programmable graphics generator" (the Atari 400/800 hardware
platform).

September 11: Atari Games, Inc. (the former Atari, Inc.) was awarded U.S.
patent 4,471,464 for 15 claims by inventors Steven T. Mayer, Jay G. Miner,
Douglas G. Neubauer, and Joseph C. Decuir regarding their "Data processing
system with programmable graphics generator" (the Atari 400/800 hardware
platform).

September 20: Neil Harris, previously of Commodore International (software
division), joined Atari as director of communications (manager of publications
and user group support).  With Atari director of creative services Mel
Stevens, Harris would be responsible for launching a replacement for the
former Atari, Inc. magazine, Atari Connection, to be called: Atari Explorer.

September 25: Rather than halt production of Atari's 800XL home computer and
its 2600 video-game player, as many had expected, Atari has significantly
expanded production of the two products, Sam Tramiel said (interviewed in
Taipei by the Dow Jones Service). "In January, Atari will introduce a second
low-priced computer that will run games and software made for the predecessor
product."  (The Globe and Mail (Canada)) 

October 9: Date of Atari internal draft specification document for a "900XLA"
computer (earlier: XL/M; later: 65XEM).  The document contrasted the
"900XLA" with the forthcoming "900XL" computer (which would ship as: 65XE).
https://atariage.com/forums/topic/78378-atari-900xla-product-spec/

Europe, in addition to new production 800XL computers and 1050 disk drives,

supply 600XL/800XL systems and software largely from existing inventories.
